title: What C2PA, watermarks and metadata can tell you
body_md:
## A passport stamp is not a character reference

A stamp in a passport proves that someone crossed a border on a given day. It says nothing about why they travelled, or whether they told the officer the truth. Provenance signals on a photo or a clip work the same way: they record where a file has been, and stay silent about what it shows.

So a file can look authentic and still carry a false claim, and a genuine photo can reach you with every trace of its origin stripped by a chat app. Provenance answers one question, about the file's source and edits. It leaves three open: whether the scene happened, whether the caption is honest, and whether anybody has authorised the payment you are being asked to make.

**C2PA Content Credentials** are signed records (manifests) attached to media. A compatible viewer can check that the signed statements belong to this exact file and show the tools and edits the maker declared. The C2PA v2.4 explainer is plain about the limit: validation shows that the provenance is well-formed and untampered under a trust model, not that the content is true. A creator can sign a staged scene. A file can be edited in a tool that records nothing. A screenshot, or a platform re-encoding the video, may shed the manifest altogether, and a missing credential is not evidence of a fake. Ask who signed, what they assert, whether the chain has gaps, and whether this is the original file.

**Watermarks** are a separate signal. A visible one can be cropped out. An invisible one, such as Google SynthID, is built into what supported tools generate and is read by that system's own detection tools. A hit gives you a narrow claim about origin, and only about that one system. A miss tells you little: the clip may come from another generator, the mark may have been removed, or the file may have passed through a workflow the checker does not support. Keep private family footage out of outside checkers.

**Ordinary metadata**, such as a timestamp or a camera model, can be edited or stripped. A mismatch is a lead; an empty field settles nothing. A reverse image search may find an earlier appearance of the picture, though old images are sometimes honestly reused as illustration, and it cannot say whether a new caption is true. For that, compare with a source you found yourself, above all before forwarding a crisis claim or acting on a financial instruction.

### Four rungs, and a place to stop

Save the original file if you can. Open any credentials in a viewer you trust. Look for earlier publication and for context. Then confirm the claim with its supposed publisher, through a channel you already know.

If the evidence gives out before the top, stop at “unverified”. It is an honest place to stand, and while you do, the clip stays unforwarded and the fee unpaid.

widget_config.goal: Read credentials, watermarks and metadata as narrow clues about where a file came from, never as a promise that it is true or that the person in it is who they claim.
widget_config.today_action: Take one public image, find the page where it was first published, and set it beside the copy that was shared with you. Write down what changed around it.
widget_config.scope: C2PA v2.4 and one product-specific watermark example, checked 20 October 2026. Support, viewers’ trust lists and the way platforms handle media all vary. The cases and the exercise below are invented.

sources.title: C2PA v2.4: the Content Credentials explainer
sources.scope: Explainer for version 2.4, viewed 20 October 2026. Signed provenance can be checked, but it does not establish factual truth, a complete history, or identity beyond its trust model.

sources.title: Google DeepMind: SynthID
sources.scope: Product page, viewed 20 October 2026. It describes marking of content from supported Google and partner products, not universal detection of AI media.

blocks.title: A real building, a false fire
blocks.situation: A post shares a signed photo of a real building and says it shows a fire burning today. The Content Credential says the photo was taken years ago.
blocks.analysis: A valid provenance record exposes the date mismatch, but it cannot fact-check the claim about today’s fire. Look for current reports from independent sources. The photo is genuine and the signature is real; the caption is what misleads.

blocks.title: The friend’s screenshot
blocks.situation: A friend sends a screenshot of a photo they took on an older phone. By the time it has been through the chat app, no Content Credential and no EXIF data (the camera details stored inside a photo file) are left.
blocks.analysis: Plenty of ordinary workflows strip this information, so its absence says nothing about manipulation. If it matters, ask for the original and check the context with your friend on a number you already have. Keep private material out of public tools unless its owner agrees.

blocks.title: Breaking news, with a fee attached
blocks.setup: An invented scenario: a short public clip claims that a local official has announced an immediate fee. You can inspect the file and its publisher, and you must decide whether to share the clip or pay. Each decision is a fresh start; nothing you paid or shared in one carries into the next.

steps.prompt: The repost carries no credential. What does that tell you?

choices.consequence: A clip that may well be genuine gets thrown out because a label went missing.
choices.explanation: A missing credential is not proof of fabrication.

choices.text: It is unverified; look for the original publication.
choices.consequence: A missing label stays a missing label, and does not become a verdict.
choices.explanation: Reposting or re-encoding can strip provenance information.

steps.prompt: A fresh start: you have paid nothing and shared nothing. This time you hold the original file, with a valid signer and an editing record. What do you do?

choices.text: Pay, because the signature backs up the fee.
choices.consequence: You send money for a fee that may still be made up, or pinned to the wrong footage.
choices.explanation: A signed file can carry claims that are false or beside the point.

choices.text: Read who signed and what is claimed, then check the fee somewhere else.
choices.consequence: You learn the file’s history without mistaking it for law or policy.
choices.explanation: A credential describes provenance. It does not say whether what was spoken is true.

steps.prompt: A fresh start: nothing paid, nothing shared. A watermark checker finds no match in a copy of the clip. What next?

choices.text: Take it as a narrow result and confirm through the official channel.
choices.consequence: One tool’s silence does not harden into a sweeping conclusion.
choices.explanation: The checker looks for the marks it supports, not for every generator or every edited copy.

choices.text: Share the clip and pay: it is proven to be human-made.
choices.consequence: You send the money and spread a clip that may be generated or miscaptioned.
choices.explanation: Finding no mark certifies nothing about authenticity.

blocks.debrief: Sometimes the sturdiest conclusion on offer is “not yet verified”. A credential, a watermark and a metadata field each answer a question smaller than “is this true?”, and every wrong turn above was a jump from the small answer to the big one. Go back and find the jumps.

questions.prompt: A C2PA credential validates on a photo of a staged scene. What has been established?

choices.text: The signed provenance claims belong to this file, under the viewer’s trust model.
choices.explanation: A valid signature does not turn a staged scene into a real one.

choices.text: The event happened exactly as claimed.
choices.explanation: Provenance covers the file’s history, not the truth of what it shows.

questions.prompt: A screenshot from a chat has no metadata. Which conclusion is justified?

choices.text: The metadata is simply gone; look for the original or for other context.
choices.explanation: Chat apps and other sharing routes often discard file metadata.
Missing metadata says nothing about how an image was made.

questions.prompt: A supported watermark is found in a clip. What can that support?

choices.text: That every statement in the clip is false.
choices.explanation: A marked clip can contain accurate statements, or serve as a legitimate illustration.

choices.text: A narrow link to the marking system, not the truth of the caption.
choices.explanation: Where a clip came from and whether its claims hold up are separate questions.
